justice: The street allocates most visible space to multiple motor-vehicle lanes, while pedestrian space is limited to narrow side sidewalks and service paths at the edges.
A side path and sidewalk are present on the right side, showing some provision for non-motorized users, but they are clearly secondary compared with the very wide carriageway.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossing facilities can be identified in the image, so accessibility appears only partial for a broad range of users.
The central median and separated edge spaces organize traffic efficiently, but the spatial balance still favors through-movement of cars over equal access for all users.
safety: Lane markings are clear and the roadway is wide and orderly, which supports predictable vehicle movement and reduces immediate conflict risk for drivers.
A planted median separates opposing traffic streams, lowering head-on conflict potential on this broad corridor.
Streetlights are installed along the road, which suggests some nighttime safety support even though current daylight conditions limit full assessment.
The apparent side path on the right is separated from the main carriageway by a curb and green strip, reducing direct exposure of pedestrians or cyclists to fast traffic.
However, the road geometry is very wide and straight, which may encourage higher vehicle speeds and create safety concerns for any users needing to cross.
livability: The corridor appears dominated by transport infrastructure, with overpasses, wide lanes, and a large median, giving it a functional rather than socially active character.
There are very few visible shops, active frontages, or public gathering places; the only building frontage on the left is sparse and set back from the street.
Large stretches of roadside greenery and trees improve environmental quality, but they do not by themselves create a lively or socially interactive street.
No visible benches, kiosks, bus stop shelters, or plaza-like spaces are present, limiting everyday street life and casual social use.
sustainability: The presence of trees and planted strips along both sides contributes to urban greening and some ecological value.
The landscaped median and roadside planting may help with dust control and visual softening, although the large bare-soil median section is less effective than dense vegetation would be.
A separated side path on the right provides at least some infrastructure for non-motorized travel, which is more sustainable than a car-only corridor.
At the same time, the overall design remains heavily road-oriented, with extensive paved space for motor vehicles that likely supports high car dependence.
aesthetics: The roadway surface is clean and newly maintained, giving the corridor a neat and orderly appearance.
Rows of trees and low shrubs on both sides add visual softness and reduce the harshness of the wide asphalt roadway.
The overpass structures and long open corridor create a coherent but utilitarian visual character rather than a richly textured streetscape.
The large exposed soil median in the foreground detracts from visual quality compared with a fully planted or finished central landscape.
comfort: Trees line both sides of the street, offering some shade potential for side paths and sidewalks, but the main corridor remains highly exposed to sun due to its great width and open sky.
The sidewalks and side paths appear smooth and unobstructed, which supports basic physical comfort for walking or rolling.
No visible seating, shelters, or resting facilities are provided along the edge spaces, reducing comfort for users spending time outside vehicles.
The broad separation between modes can improve psychological comfort by distancing pedestrians from moving traffic, but the scale of the road and overpass environment may still feel inhospitable.
Traffic seems light at the moment, which may lower noise and stress compared with a congested arterial.
walkability: A sidewalk or walking path is visible along the right side, so pedestrian movement is physically possible along the corridor.
The pedestrian realm appears continuous in this view, without obvious parked vehicles or clutter blocking the walking path.
However, the street is extremely wide and vehicle-oriented, making the overall environment less inviting for walking despite the presence of edge sidewalks.
No visible marked crosswalks, pedestrian signals, or refuge points are shown, which weakens connectivity for walking across or between sides of the road.
The lack of active street frontage, seating, and destinations reduces the attractiveness of walking for daily use.
bikeability: A narrow side lane or path on the right may accommodate cycling, and it is spatially separated from the main vehicle lanes by curb and planting.
The separation from fast motor traffic improves perceived safety compared with sharing the main carriageway.
However, no clear bicycle symbols, colored bike-lane markings, or dedicated cycling signage are visible, so the cycling function is ambiguous.
The road corridor is long, wide, and designed mainly for motorized flow, which may discourage less confident cyclists.
No bicycle parking, intersection bicycle boxes, or other supporting cycling facilities are visible in the scene.
